flashcards.q: What is a warp and how does SIMT execution work?
flashcards.a: A fixed group of 32 threads on an SM that execute the same instruction in lockstep, sharing one instruction fetch/decode unit -- threads not on the active path are masked off, not truly parallel.

flashcards.q: Why does warp divergence cost real cycles?
flashcards.a: When threads in a warp take different branches, the hardware serializes: runs the if-path with else-taking threads masked off, then the else-path with if-taking threads masked off -- a 2-way divergence costs roughly 2x the cycles of no divergence.

flashcards.q: What is occupancy and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: The ratio of resident warps to the max an SM can host (64/SM on H100). High occupancy lets the scheduler switch to a different ready warp at ~0 cost when one stalls on memory, hiding HBM latency instead of leaving the SM idle.

flashcards.q: Why is a GPU warp switch essentially free, unlike a CPU thread context switch?
flashcards.a: Every resident warp's full register state lives permanently and simultaneously in the SM's register file -- there's nothing to save or restore, just a scheduling decision about which resident warp's registers to read next.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't nvidia-smi utilization percentage indicate compute efficiency?
flashcards.a: It reports whether any kernel is running during the sampling window, not how efficiently it uses compute -- a memory-bandwidth-bound kernel can show 100% utilization while compute units sit substantially idle waiting on HBM.

flashcards.q: What is arithmetic intensity and what does it determine?
flashcards.a: FLOPs performed per byte of data moved from memory. Compared against the GPU's compute-to-bandwidth ridge point, it determines whether a kernel is compute-bound or memory-bandwidth-bound.

flashcards.q: Why is LLM inference at batch size 1 memory-bandwidth-bound?
flashcards.a: Generating one token requires loading the entire model's weights from HBM but performs relatively few FLOPs per token relative to that data volume -- low arithmetic intensity leaves compute units mostly idle.

flashcards.q: How does batching fix the memory-bandwidth-bound problem in LLM inference?
flashcards.a: The same weight-loading cost from HBM is amortized across many requests' compute in one kernel launch, raising arithmetic intensity and pushing the workload toward compute-bound, extracting more useful tokens per GPU-hour.

flashcards.q: What is continuous batching and why does it beat static batching?
flashcards.a: Static batching waits for every request in a fixed group to finish, wasting slots on early-finishing short requests. Continuous batching swaps finished requests out and new ones in at every decode step, keeping the batch continuously full of active work.

flashcards.q: What throughput gains are reported for continuous batching?
flashcards.a: vLLM reports up to ~23x throughput with reduced p50 latency vs naive serving; the Orca paper reported up to ~36.9x vs static batching in its benchmarks.

flashcards.q: What does PagedAttention solve, distinct from continuous batching?
flashcards.a: It manages the KV cache in fixed-size, non-contiguous pages (like OS virtual memory) instead of one large contiguous block sized for max sequence length, reducing fragmentation so more requests' KV caches fit simultaneously, enabling bigger effective batch sizes.

flashcards.q: What is kernel launch overhead and why does it matter for real workloads?
flashcards.a: Roughly 3-10 microseconds fixed cost per launch even for a minimal kernel; a workload issuing thousands of small sequential kernels pays this repeatedly, and it dominates total cost when it exceeds per-kernel compute time -- fixed by kernel fusion.

flashcards.q: What are Tensor Cores and why do they matter for mixed-precision ML?
flashcards.a: Dedicated matrix-multiply-accumulate hardware (introduced Volta, 2017) optimized for fp16/bf16/fp8, far more efficient per cycle than composing matmul from general CUDA cores -- the actual mechanism delivering reduced-precision throughput gains.
